This page records why the lab's notes write certain symbols the way they do.
Each entry states our convention, the reasons for it, and the other conventions you will meet in other sources.
Notes sites can link to an entry here instead of keeping their own copy.

## The vector mark {#sec-vector-mark}

Our convention is a tilde under the letter, as in $\vx$.
The shared macro `\vecf` (and shortcuts such as `\vx` and `\vbeta`) prints it.

We chose a mark underneath for three reasons.

-   Bold letters are hard to write by hand.
    When we work problems by hand, for example on a board, a bold letter is hard to copy neatly with chalk or a marker.
    A small tilde under a letter is quick to write, so the handwritten symbol and the printed symbol look the same.
-   The space above a letter is already used.
    In statistics, a hat over a symbol means "estimated value".
    A vector mark above the letter would have to share that space with the hat, and the two marks would be crowded together.
-   A mark below the letter stays in place when we add a hat.
    The vector mark stays below and the estimate mark stays above, so each mark can be read on its own.

::: {#exm-estimated-vector-notation}
##### An estimated vector

Suppose a regression model has a coefficient vector $\vbeta$ with $p$ entries.
Its estimate from data is written $\hvb$, with the hat above the symbol and the vector mark below it.
We read $\hvb$ as "the estimated vector $\vbeta$".
Its $j$-th entry is the estimate of the $j$-th coefficient.
That entry is a single number, so it needs no vector mark, only the hat.
:::

Other sources use bold letters ($\mathbf{x}$) or arrows ($\overrightarrow{x}$) for the same objects.
All of these notations mark a vector.

## Subscripts and parentheses {#sec-subscripts-parentheses}

Our convention splits the work between a subscript and parentheses.
An indexed family is a collection of objects labeled by an index.
A subscript names which member of an indexed family we mean.
A subscript holds an index, such as the $i$ in $x_i$,
or a parameter that picks one function or distribution out of a family, such as the $\theta$ in $f_\theta$.
Parentheses hold the input a function is evaluated at, as in $f(x)$.
So $f_\theta(x)$ reads "the member of the family labeled $\theta$, evaluated at $x$".

We chose this split for one reason.
Each slot then answers one question about the symbol, so once you know the split, you can tell what each part of a symbol is doing.

Nothing forces the split.
Sources divide the work differently, and you will meet the same objects written the other way around.
When you read a formula from another source, first work out what each subscript and each input in parentheses is doing:
labeling a member of an indexed family, or being the input of a function.
That tells you which convention the source follows, whatever its layout.

::: {#exm-stochastic-process-slots}
##### A stochastic process uses both slots

A random experiment is a process that involves chance, such as a coin flip, and an outcome $\omega$ is one possible result of it.
A random variable is a function whose input is an outcome $\omega$.
A stochastic process is an indexed family of random variables $X_t$, one for each index $t$, such as a time.
The index goes in the subscript, because it picks a member of the family.
Each $X_t$ is itself a function of the outcome $\omega$, so the outcome goes in the parentheses: $X_t(\omega)$.
Fixing $\omega$ and letting $t$ vary gives one ordinary function of $t$, called a path of the process.
Many sources drop $\omega$ and write $X_t$.
Others write $X(t)$, often when $t$ is continuous, which puts the index in the parentheses instead of the subscript.
:::

## Binary labels {#sec-binary-labels}

A binary classification problem has two classes, and each observation carries a label that names its class.
Our convention is to code the labels as $0$ and $1$, as in logistic regression, where the label $1$ means the event happened.
The chapter on support vector machines switches to the labels $-1$ and $+1$, and says so where it does.

We switch to $-1$ and $+1$ for support vector machines for one reason.
A classifier outputs a number.
It predicts the class $+1$ when the number is positive, and the class $-1$ when the number is negative.
With $\pm 1$ labels, a prediction is correct when the output and the label have the same sign.
So the product of the label and the output is positive for a correct prediction and negative for a wrong one.
The size of the product measures how far the output is from zero, on the correct side when the prediction is correct.
With $0$ and $1$ labels, the same test needs two cases.
If the output is a probability, a correct prediction is an output above $0.5$ with the label $1$, or an output below $0.5$ with the label $0$.

Both codings describe the same data.
Other sources pick one coding and use it everywhere, so check which one a formula assumes before comparing it with ours.

## The intercept {#sec-intercept}

A linear model for an outcome adds up the inputs times their coefficients, and then adds one more number that does not multiply any input.
That number is the intercept.
Our convention is to write the intercept separately, as $\coef{0}$.
The coefficient vector $\vcoef$ then holds the slopes only, meaning the coefficients that multiply the inputs.
The input vector $\vpredvar$ holds the inputs.

We call the number $\coef{0} + \dprod{\vcoef}{\vpredvar}$ the score here.
This is not the score of statistics, which is a different quantity.
Logistic regression applies one more function to the score to get a probability.

Writing the intercept separately keeps it visible as its own number.
In logistic regression, for example, the intercept shifts the decision boundary, the set of inputs where the model is undecided between the two classes, while the slopes tilt it.

Other sources absorb the intercept.
They add a constant input $1$ to the start of the input vector, and the coefficient vector then also holds the intercept, at its start.
The score is then $\dprod{\vcoef}{\vpredvar}$ alone.
Both forms describe the same model.
When you meet a score written as $\dprod{\vcoef}{\vpredvar}$, check whether the input vector starts with a constant $1$.

## Counting the layers of a neural network {#sec-counting-layers}

A neural network passes its input through a sequence of layers.
Each layer is a row of units, and each unit computes one number.
Between two neighboring layers, a weight matrix holds the numbers that say how much each unit in the first layer contributes to each unit in the second.

Suppose a network has an input layer, one hidden layer (a layer between the input and the output), and an output layer.
Some sources call it a three-layer network, because it has three rows of units.
Our convention is to call it a two-layer network.
Here "two-layer" counts the weight matrices, not the rows of units.
The network has two weight matrices: input to hidden, and hidden to output.
We can also say that it has one hidden layer.

We chose to count the weight matrices because the input layer has no weights of its own and does no computation.
Its values are the data.
Each weight matrix is one computation from one row of units to the next, so counting the weight matrices counts the steps that do work.
This is a choice, not a requirement, and both names are in use.
Check which one a source means before comparing the depths of two networks.

## Conventions for cross-entropy {#sec-cross-entropy-conventions}

Cross-entropy is a measure of how well a model's predicted probabilities match the observed labels.
For labeled data, it adds up the negative logarithms of the probabilities the model gave to the labels that were observed.
A lower cross-entropy means a better match.
Two choices change its numerical value without changing which of two models it prefers on the same data.

The first choice is the base of the logarithm.
The base is free, so state it whenever you quote a number.
Base $e$ gives units called nats, and base $2$ gives units called bits.
Take a two-class model that gives probability $0.5$ to each class.
For a single example, its cross-entropy is $\log_e 2 \approx 0.693$ nats, or $\log_2 2 = 1$ bit.
Changing the base multiplies every cross-entropy by the same positive constant, so it cannot change which of two classifiers you would pick.
It does change the number, so a cross-entropy quoted without its base cannot be checked against a number from another source.

The second choice is whether to sum or to average over the examples.
Our convention is to sum over all examples.
Some software reports the average under the same name.
On the same data, dividing every cross-entropy by the number of examples does not change which of two models is preferred, but it does change the number.
So also check whether a source reports the sum or the average before comparing its numbers with ours.

## Names for the same object in machine learning and statistics {#sec-ml-statistics-names}

Machine learning and statistics texts often use different names and symbols for the same object.
Each chapter of our notes says which symbols it uses.
For example, the chapter on neural networks writes $\vw$ and $b$, and the regression chapters write $\vcoef$ and $\coef{0}$.

-   A linear function is written $f(\vx) = \dprod{\vw}{\vx} + b$ in neural network texts.
    There $\vw$ holds the weights, and $b$ is the bias, which plays the role of the intercept.
    This "bias" is a different idea from the bias of an estimator in statistics.
    Statistics texts write the coefficients as $\vbeta$ and the intercept as $\beta_0$, as in [the intercept entry](#sec-intercept).
    The two notations describe the same linear model.
-   Machine learning texts often write $D$ or $d$ for the number of inputs and $N$ for the number of observations.
    Statistics texts write $n$ for the number of observations and $p$ for the number of inputs, which they call predictors.
-   Neural network and pattern recognition texts often call the label the target.
    Statistics texts call it the response or the outcome.
    In classification, all of these names mean the same object as our label.

You will read both literatures, so expect to meet both sets of names and symbols.

## Writing the likelihood function {#sec-likelihood-notation}

The likelihood function is a function of the model's parameters, with the observed data held fixed.
Our convention is mostly $\Lik(\theta)$, which leaves the data implicit.
We use a form that shows the data, such as $\Lik(\theta; \vx)$, when we want to name which data set the likelihood is computed from.
We chose $\Lik(\theta)$ to emphasize that the likelihood is a function of the parameters.

Other sources write the same likelihood in other ways:

-   $\Lik(\vx; \theta)$.
-   $\Lik_{\vx}(\theta)$.
-   $\Lik(\vx \mid \theta)$ or $\Lik_{\theta}(\vx)$.

We read every one of these forms as the likelihood: $\vx$ is the observed data, held fixed, and $\theta$ is the input that varies.
The forms $\Lik(\vx \mid \theta)$ and $\Lik_{\theta}(\vx)$ write the data where a formula for the distribution of the data would write it.
That formula is a function of the data, with the parameter held fixed.
The likelihood uses the same formula, but treats the parameter as the input and holds the data fixed.
So when a source writes one of these two forms, check that it means a function of $\theta$.

## Writing the score function {#sec-score-notation}

The log-likelihood is the natural logarithm of the likelihood function.
The score function is the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter.
This is the score of statistics, which is not the linear score of [the intercept entry](#sec-intercept).
When the model has several parameters, the score is a vector that holds one partial derivative for each parameter, taken with the other parameters held fixed.
We often omit its arguments and write $\score$ for $\score(\theta)$.
When we want to show the data, we write $\score(\theta; \vx)$, in the same style as the likelihood.

Some sources write $U$ or $S$ for the score function instead.
We write $\score$ because it keeps $U$ and $S$ free for other uses.

## Symbols for estimands and estimators {#sec-estimand-estimator-symbols}

An estimand is the quantity we want to learn about, and an estimator is a rule that computes a guess of it from data.

Our convention is to write estimands with lower-case Greek letters, such as $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$.
We write an estimator by placing a hat over the symbol of its estimand, as in $\hat\theta$.
Usually the dependence of the estimator on the data is left implicit.

Other sources use other symbols, so check which symbol a source uses for the estimand before reading a formula.

## Short symbols for the pieces of the bias-variance decomposition {#sec-bias-variance-symbols}

Fix a covariate value $\predvar$, a training sample size, and a fitting procedure.
The fitted prediction function $\predfn$ varies from one training data set to the next.
Let $\Outvar$ be a new outcome at $\predvar$, independent of the training data.
Write $\truemeanf{\predvar}$ for the mean of $\Outvar$.
The noise is the random part of $\Outvar$ that no function of the covariates predicts.
Three short symbols name the pieces of the expected squared error in predicting $\Outvar$:

-   The bias of the fitted value at $\predvar$ is $\biassymf{\predfn\paren{\predvar}}$, from the macro `\biassymf`.
    It is the mean of the fitted value over training data sets, minus the true mean $\truemeanf{\predvar}$.
    This is the expected error of the fitted value as an estimate of the true mean.
    The long operator $\Biast$ stays available for the full definition.
-   The variance of the fitted value over training data sets is $\varsymf{\predfn\paren{\predvar}}$, from the macro `\varsymf`.
    The macro `\varsymf` is a variance operator for any random variable, in the style of the expectation $\E{\cdot}$.
-   The irreducible error is $\irrerr$, from the macro `\irrerr`.
    It is the variance of the noise, so it is the existing variance parameter $\varpar$.
    When the noise variance depends on $\predvar$, the irreducible error is a function of $\predvar$.

With these symbols, the expected squared error splits into three pieces, where the expectation is over the training data and over $\Outvar$:

$$
\E{\paren{\Outvar - \predfn\paren{\predvar}}^2} = \biassymf{\predfn\paren{\predvar}}^2 + \varsymf{\predfn\paren{\predvar}} + \irrerr.
$$

A derivation that does not manipulate a piece can write its short symbol, after the piece is defined in full.
Each piece is a population quantity.
It is a fixed number once $\predvar$, the population, the fitting procedure and the training sample size are fixed.

We write the bias and the variance with upright Latin letters, in the style of the expectation $\E{\cdot}$.
We make this exception to the Greek convention for estimands in [the estimands entry](#sec-estimand-estimator-symbols).
The variance operator applies to any random variable, not only to a fitted value.
The bias operator is applied to an estimator, and its letter matches the name of the long operator $\Biast$.
Like the expectation, each has two macros.
The macros `\biassym` and `\varsym` print the bare operators $\biassym$ and $\varsym$, as `\Expp` prints $\Expp$.
The macros `\biassymf` and `\varsymf` apply the operator to an argument in square brackets, as `\E` does.

These Latin letters have collisions:

-   The macros `\Regcoef` and `\Coef` also print an upright $\Regcoef$, for regression coefficients.
    So avoid using `\biassym` or `\biassymf` together with either of them in one document.
-   The existing macro `\V` prints $\V$, the full name of the variance, so `\varsymf` is the short form, not a replacement.

The irreducible error keeps a Greek letter, because it is a variance parameter and not an operator.
It reuses $\sigma^2$, which already names the variance parameter, instead of getting a new letter.

Some sources write the same pieces in other ways:

-   They keep the operator form, as in $\Biast(\hat f(x))^2$ and $\Vart(\hat f(x))$, in every line of the derivation.
    This is unambiguous but long.
-   They write $\sigma_\epsilon^2$ or $\Vart(\epsilon)$ for the irreducible error, where $\epsilon$ is their noise symbol.
-   They may use a lower-case Latin letter for each piece.
    We avoid this because $b$ already names the bias of a neural network in [the names entry](#sec-ml-statistics-names), and the macro `\vv` prints the vector $\vv$.

Check which form a source uses before comparing its decomposition with ours.

## Probability notation {#sec-probability-notation}

A random variable is a function of the outcome of a random experiment, as in [the stochastic process example](#exm-stochastic-process-slots).
Its value depends on chance.
Our convention is to write random variables with uppercase letters, such as $X$, $Y$ and $Z$, and their observed values with the matching lowercase letters, such as $x$, $y$ and $z$.
Some sources keep uppercase letters for matrices, and use other symbols for random variables.
Check a source's own notation section before assuming ours.

An event is something that may or may not happen, such as $X > 2$.
A probability mass function gives the probability of each value of a discrete random variable, one that takes separate values such as $0, 1, 2$.
A probability density describes a continuous random variable, one that takes values on a continuous range, such as a height.

We write $\Pr()$ for the probability of an event, and $\p()$ for a probability mass function or a probability density.
Here $\p$ is a function name, not the number of inputs.
Some sources write $P()$ for all of these.
Others keep $f()$ for densities and mass functions, and use $P()$ only for the probability of an event.

We write the expectation of a random variable with square brackets, as in $\E{X}$.
Some sources write blackboard bold $\mathbb{E}[X]$, or parentheses, $E(X)$.
The meaning is the same.

We write $X \ind Y$ for "$X$ is independent of $Y$".
Some sources write $X \perp Y$, or state independence only in words.

We write $\neg A$ for the complement of an event $A$, read "not $A$".
Some sources write $A^c$ or $\bar{A}$.

We write $\eqdef$ for an equality that holds by definition.
This tells it apart from an equality that follows from other facts.
Some sources use a bare $=$ for both.
